t: When You Find Yourself Far Behind, Reset the Clock
q: When teams get blown away and find themselves in a lopsided game, the best coaches take a pause (halftime) and reset the score to 0-0.
People naturally feel hopeless and become demotivated whenever they are significantly behind in their commitments, goals, and desired outcomes.

Mentally resetting the score or clock allows performers to reframe the situation as a fresh start and to focus their attention on immediate effort and improvement instead of the daunting challenge of catching up.
Going from outcome-focused to process-oriented restores confidence and makes it easier to bounce back from any new obstacle or adversity.
People perform best when they focus on process over outcomes.

t: Creating New Habits Requires a Daily Rhythm
q: What isn’t obvious is how frequently the routine needs to be repeated before a habit is formed. New behaviors that don’t occur daily seldom become habits.
The research confirms that doing anything new once a day for a week is far superior to doing something new seven times in one day once a week.
Daily repetition enhances motivation, reinforces memory and learning, and encourages quick error correction.
When the opportunity set to apply the new behavior appears limited, it is up to the habit-maker to find other avenues and practice options.
What is critical for inculcating a new habit is the daily repetition.

t: What's the Difference Between an A-Player and the B's & C's
q: Here's a simple scheme: A-players just need a goal. Once they know the desired outcome, they can figure out how to get there.
B-players need the goal and the strategy or approach to achieve it. They depend on leaders to help them think through the various choices or options and what game plan is best to ensure success.
C-players need more than the goal and the strategy. They need the tactics, too.

B-players need practice thinking of strategies and approaches to problems and goals. Dissecting existing strategies and creating new ones is how B-players gain the confidence and acumen to fly on their own.
Good leaders do more than simply recruit A-players to join their teams. They do the hard work it takes to elevate the talents, skills, and potential of everyone on the team, including the C-players.

t: How Teachers Mess Up The Amazing Benefits Of Routines
q: The students were relatively well behaved but distracted—staring off into the distance, bumping into each other, lost in thought.
Yet, spend a couple of hours on any school campus and most routines look just like this, even with much older students.
Which is a bright red flashing sign that the students are very effectively learning how to be helpless and dependent on others, even for the simplest things like walking to lunch or opening a laptop.
The truth is that routines are one of the best opportunities teachers have to impact students and change them for the better.
But her approach, her aggressively doing and doing for her students, was hurting them. It was holding them back.
Routines are a means to an end. But the end isn’t the lunchroom or their seats after a transition. It’s the lessons they offer, which when allowed and nourished by the teacher, can be profound.

t: Micro-Goals Get Projects and People Back on Track
q: Team members who are stalled, delayed, or slow typically have lost sight of these steps or have failed to focus on the micro-steps or goals that make them up.
Instead of focusing on a distant and somewhat intimidating objective, micro-goals break that objective down into tiny, actionable tasks that can be completed more easily and quickly.
Studies show that micro-goals bypass the psychological barriers some team members experience when approaching a larger task.
When team members are really lost or stuck, good leaders avoid the temptation to point to more than one micro-goal at a time.
The best leaders know that the smallest goal can sometimes be the largest motivation.

t: How Leaders Unwittingly Create Entitlement
q: When they fail to tie their caring and rewards to measurable goals, a sense of entitlement is usually the result.
Entitlement is an organizational disease caused by leaders. People learn to be entitled. They don’t show up that way. They simply respond to how they are treated.

Leaders who fall into this trap often do so to increase morale and job satisfaction. To gain favor, they lower expectations, avoid giving critical feedback, recognize people for mediocre work, and provide special accommodations and treatment to anyone who asks for it.
Productivity drops like an anchor, while complaining about whatever expectations still exist goes up.
Entitlement can’t exist when standards and expectations for performance remain high and the most deserving team members receive the hard-won recognition they have earned.

t: What Students Want, According to a Survey
q: 82% of students felt more encouraged to learn when their teacher is passionate about the subject.
Passion is part of the CCP of Credibility. Thankfully, passion can be demonstrated by more than just over-the-top enthusiasm (my personality doesn’t tend toward much of that).
72% of students said a teacher helped them enjoy a subject they didn’t expect to like or thought they weren’t good at. This is the language of Value.
90% of students said having a teacher who cares about their emotional well-being helps them do better in school.
92% of students said they notice the hard work teachers put into their work. I love this. Almost every student surveyed said they can see the work we put in.
students want what we want: enjoyable and productive learning experiences. They WANT us to succeed. They WANT to WANT to learn.

t: People Who Complain Incessantly About a Problem Before Addressing It
q: Insisting on complaining about a problem (and the people who created it) before attempting to solve it is a mindset that fixates on what is wrong rather than how to address it.
By detailing the negatives surrounding the problem, these colleagues elevate their own self-worth and demonstrate to others how important they are in the process.
If given the option, they would prefer to work with someone else. They would rather not stomach the negativity and grousing that wastes time and drains others emotionally.
The second plumber arrives, examines the pipes, tells you what they plan to do, and then gets busy fixing the problem.

Convincing a complainer that they create an unproductive climate with their incessant whining isn’t easy. They have trained themselves to operate from this mindset, so it is difficult for them to grasp or make a change.

t: It's Time to Conduct a Distraction Audit
q: Even small distractions cause people to take longer to finish tasks and degrade the quality of the output.
When attention is divided, the brain must reallocate resources, which slows down work, impairs memory and retention, and leads to more errors.
Distractions are a coping mechanism for many people. We distract ourselves on purpose to regulate our stress, emotions, and anxiety.
If you’re serious about becoming more productive, the first step is to conduct a distraction audit.
By logging every interruption or distraction over a set period, patterns will begin to emerge. Focus on those distractions that are unnecessary and negatively impact your work.

t: Leaders Who Make Fun of Themselves Build Trust and Comfort
q: This is because self-deprecation disarms people and makes leaders more relatable and personable. People tend to trust leaders they find more likable.
By humorously acknowledging their own flaws, shortcomings, or mistakes, leaders show themselves to be human, which makes them more trustworthy.
Leaders should never attempt self-deprecation that goes too far by disclosing serious doubt or incompetence.

This perception is amplified for leaders of higher status. When others hold a leader in high regard or they have a significant title, position, or authority, self-deprecating remarks show them to be imperfect and serve to make people around them more secure.
Remember this: If you take yourself too seriously all of the time, others won’t.

t: If You Don't Believe Me, Maybe It's Time to Ask Your Peers
q: Team members who dig in and refuse to yield to feedback that is obvious to everyone but themselves offer quite a challenge for leaders.
Common among the reasons for rejecting this feedback is usually a lack of self-awareness.
Savvy leaders have a trick up their sleeves when dealing with a recalcitrant team member who ignores their feedback. They send them on a hunt to learn what others think.
In cases where the peers may be reserved in their answers, the leader might prepare them for the conversation and ask them to help their teammate by being highly candid.
Once the incredulous team member has completed the brief interviews, they normally have a much different view. The negative impact they are having will create an echo that shakes them up.

t: 21 Annoying Student Behaviors That Are Indeed Enforceable
q: Teachers ask me frequently if minor but annoying student behaviors are enforceable.
Although SCM allows you to create the exact classroom you want, personally I would enforce a consequence in response to every behavior on the list.
Your students must know what is and isn’t okay so well that all 21 are obvious. Even if each one isn’t expressly stated.
For example, kicking a classmate in line isn’t something you have to define as against the rules. It clearly is. No explanation is needed.
A bigger concern than whether students know what types and categories of behaviors are unacceptable is whether you do.

t: Leaders Who Refuse to Submit to the Mob
q: While it is essential to consider all the stakeholders impacted by a decision, leaders must draw on their own life experiences and judgments to inform their choices.
Everyone has opinions, and they matter, but they are not as critical as facts and data.
Looking at how each constituent base or stakeholder faction will judge the decision is usually a mistake. What will the composite view of all the voices together be over the long term?

You can always recognize a mob by an unwillingness to consider any other option, a willingness to breach social norms to get its way, the high emotional intensity of the arguments, and a fixation on a triggering event that justifies its extreme demands.
Instead, strong leaders turn the tables and say “No way” to the mob.

t: The Evidence Behind The Will to Learn
q: The only thing wrong with John Hattie’s career-long, herculean meta-analysis is that it’s too good. Visible Learning is way too good. It represents the largest scale analysis of educational research ever conducted — insanely large, as in 130,000 studies are represented in it, involving more than 400,000,000 students from around the world.

The Will to Learn is basically a book that asks, ‘What if you came up with an approach to leveraging some of the most powerful things in Visible Learning and framed it in accessible, teacher-friendly language — by a practicing teacher, for practicing teachers?
Teacher Credibility = 1.09 effect size. This one’s a whopper. And that’s one of the reasons it’s the base of the Five Key Beliefs pyramid.

All of my work has a beguiling simplicity to it. It’s so simple that it appears dumb. “We already do this,” I hear folks say. And to this I agree — many of us do do the things I recommend in The Will to Learn. The problem I’m trying to remedy is that we don’t do the things I describe in the book with the frequency and intentionality and awareness and intelligence that they merit.

Research by Hulleman and Harackiewicz (2009) found that students who wrote about how science topics applied to their lives saw 0.80 grade point improvements — demonstrating the power of value cultivation.

Walton and Cohen’s (2011) belonging interventions with African American college students resulted in 0.24 grade point improvements sustained through senior year and reduced the racial achievement gap by 52%.
Student motivation is NOT just a feel-good topic. It’s NOT a thing to touch on and move ahead to fancier things. It is fundamental.

t: Stop Trying to Fix People
q: A leader’s role is to change how people act, engage, and respond to make them more effective while at the same time accepting that many of their flaws and failings can’t be influenced or modified.
Personality traits, like introversion, are relatively stable throughout adulthood.
Leaders who attempt to “fix” qualities rooted in biology and personality are doomed to fail and make the target of their repairs feel scrutinized and disfavored.
Team members with high anxiety, emotional instability, low self-discipline, and the need to dominate, among other traits, likely render themselves incapable of performing on a team.
It’s time to change your approach. Stop trying to fix people. Coach them up instead.

t: Keeping Yourself Top of Mind
q: Reminding prospective relationships, clients, and senior leaders that you stand ready to engage with them can substantially increase the odds that they will turn toward you with an opportunity.
In the world of marketing, a brand that is top of mind for consumers enjoys increased sales and customer loyalty.
But checking in lacks authenticity in newer or unestablished relationships unless it is accompanied by something of value.
But pound-for-pound, the best way to stay top of mind is by asking for advice, guidance, help, or instruction.
Even busy and influential people feel more confident, valued, appreciated, and expert when they are asked for their advice, insight, and guidance.

t: Leaders Who Tease Others Must Be Open to Being Teased Back
q: Mutual teasing expresses closeness and signals that the parties are comfortable with each other and enjoy the mutual exchange of light humor.
Instead of expressing dissatisfaction or asking others to make a change, teasing offers the criticism wrapped in humor to make it easier to accept.
Without necessarily meaning to, leaders who tease individuals who do not feel comfortable teasing the leader back can project that they have a special status and enjoy an unequal power.
If they sense the leader may be intentionally trying to humiliate them, they will likely withdraw and stay out of target range whenever they can.
Good leaders engage more often like peers, reducing their status, so they can create the closeness they need to motivate and inspire others.

t: Using a Code Word to Help Others to Regulate Their Bad Behavior
q: The hard part is seeing their bad form while they are in action or in the throes of engaging others.

But saying so out loud can be embarrassing or off-putting. Such a spoken warning or spotlight will likely be seen as an admonishment and create defensiveness even when it has been requested by the transgressor.
The best code words are not noticed or recognized by others, but they highlight to the offender that they are repeating the mistake they have vowed not to make.
The code word asks them to pause and reflect on what they are doing. This gives them the chance to course correct and change their behavior mid-stream before real damage is done.
Before deploying this strategy, be sure to confirm with the leader or team member that they are open to this feedback in the current meeting or situation.

t: Why Accountability Isn't Working In Your Classroom
q: If accountability isn’t working in your classroom, whether individually or class wide, the problem is that you have an area of weakness.
Because it isn’t fair. It infuriates students and causes them to dislike you, distrust you, and misbehave more often.
Your students must know precisely what does and doesn’t constitute breaking each classroom rule. Gray areas equal confusion, misbehavior, and aggressive pushback when you try to enforce.
If sitting in time-out feels no different that being a regular, participating member of your class, then it won’t improve behavior.
Students are always 100 percent at fault for their own misbehavior and must be held accountable according to your classroom management plan. Full stop.

t: Leaders Who Attention Bomb
q: Attention makes people feel special, while profuse attention makes people feel obligated.
This manipulative tactic is often unconscious and deployed by leaders who are deeply insecure and crave control.
For those leaders addicted to attention bombing, they move from target to target like a child moves from one shiny new toy to another.
The predictable attention on someone new undermines the trust and confidence the team has in the leader.
Leaders who want to break the habit must first become aware of the signs and then refrain from focusing too much attention on any one team member, no matter how worthy they might seem.

t: Treating Your Team Like a Family
q: Just like in a family, leaders and teammates celebrate successes and milestones together, and share ideas, concerns, and feedback without the fear of judgment.
Family-like teams often blur the lines between personal and professional life, leading people to feel pressured to sacrifice their well-being for the team.
In a family-like setting, feedback and performance reviews become more personal rather than constructive.
Family-like teams encourage conformity and discourage dissent and disagreement. Diverse voices and viewpoints are seen as disloyal and out of step with the family.
The best leaders don’t treat work groups as families. Instead, they harvest the honey of trust and connection without recreating the hive.

t: Transparency Statements That Diffuse Distrust During Moments of Genuine Connection e-connection-mgcs
q: these brief (30- to 90-second) encounters with students can often be awkward and sometimes even threatening to students.
Researchers found that the first 45 words in an encounter between a community member and a police officer were highly predictive of the tenor and quality of the whole encounter.

Hi, Destiny, how’s it going? I’m pulling students aside this week, just trying to get to know each of you better so I can give you a good experience this year. Is it okay if I talk to you for a minute?
Timing: The statement comes right at the beginning, setting the tone for the interaction. Benevolence: Conveying an honest, positive rationale for the interaction.
Genuine: Obviously, I can’t agree with this one more, given that MGCs are meant to be real, authentic signals to students that we value, know, and respect them.
Personal and addressing the situation at hand, in the first person: “I want to be a good teacher for you.” Versus institutional, “Our school has a new initiative to get to know students.

t: Utilitarianism in Professional Relationships
q: By prioritizing personal benefits over personal attachments and emotions, these utilitarian mercenaries don’t develop authentic or rich relationships with others.
They have learned to pretend to care about others while they secretly focus only on their own desired outcomes.
Over time, people sniff out the fraud of utilitarians, many of whom can’t admit, even to themselves, that their self-interest drives everything they do in relationships.
Their “coin-operated” mentality makes everything they do about what they can get paid. This destroys the goodwill others need to support, help, and collaborate with them.
Ironically, the only way to deal effectively with a utilitarian is to act in kind.

t: What Is Your Fallback Position
q: Technically speaking, a fallback position is an alternative option or the lowest acceptable outcome the leader is willing to accept if things go terribly wrong.
Don’t confuse a fallback position with a contingency plan. Contingency plans are about risk, not failure.
Fallback plans are about failure, collapse, and defeat. If X is no longer possible or feasible, then the team resorts to fallback position Y.
It is the parachute they pack themselves just in case the plane can’t fly.
For every major decision, what is your fallback position? Sometimes, decisions and strategies blow up. Knowing your fallback position or plan can be a lifesaver.

t: Tomorrow Can Worry About Itself
q: Anyone can carry his burden, however hard, until nightfall. Anyone can do his work, however hard, for one day. Anyone can live sweetly, patiently, lovingly, purely, till the sun goes down. And this is all life really means.

the central truth is an important source of strength for both my daughter and me when we get overwhelmed: human beings are finite, time-bound creatures. We CAN worry about tomorrow, but it doesn’t DO anything.

In teaching, one of the ideas you’ve got to make peace with is that there is always more you could do. It took me my first three years of teaching, working 70+ hour workweeks, grinding myself into dust, to come to this conclusion.

In each of those three jobs, I couldn’t work at home. It was just: show up to the shift, do the things the job required, and steadily practice the knowledge and skills of the job until my capabilities increased.
It did help me go to sleep at night. It helped me learn how to let work be a work thing and life outside of work be a life-outside-of-work thing.

t: The Upside and Downside of Getting Pumped Up During Competition
q: Although common wisdom suggests getting pumped up during competition can, at certain moments, positively affect performance, research confirms that competitive arousal has more downside than upside.
Getting psyched up impairs rational and objective decision-making, narrows attention, increases risk-taking, and promotes aggressive behavior.
Once aroused, performers are more likely to fixate on winning at any cost, favoring immediate rewards over long-term benefits.
The flood of adrenaline and dopamine that performers experience during arousal makes them feel superhuman, if even for a moment.
That’s why the best performers manage their competitive arousal, preferring to stay focused and in control of their emotions in a more “controlled enthusiasm” while they perform.

t: Loneliness in a Hyperconnected Workplace
q: Despite a workplace with more opportunities for connectivity than ever, loneliness and social isolation are on the rise inside organizations of every stripe.
Instead of striving to find and create more social connections and relationships, lonely team members disengage, skip meetings whenever they can, and avoid interaction with others.
And here’s the kicker: They almost never tell others, especially leaders, that they are lonely.
The most important action is for the leader to check in frequently and to inquire about how the team member is doing inside and outside of the workplace.

The best leaders go one step further in supporting a lonely team member. They unofficially serve as a mentor to this colleague, arranging to meet on a regular basis to discuss their careers, aspirations, and interests.

t: Organizing Yourself to Delegate Effectively
q: A few days before the project that was once far away, you realize there was background, prep work, and other tasks that could have been done weeks ago to avoid having to rush it.
Because time is now of the essence, those who could have helped can no longer lend a hand.

Leaders who are overwhelmed by tasks, decisions, problems, and assignments typically focus on what they need to do and fail to chart out the steps needed for the many deliverables that are weeks or months away.
The best leaders create three distinct sets of tasks and priorities. Those that must be attended to today, those that need to be completed this week, and those that are weeks and months away.

By identifying the tasks that can be completed now, leaders have the option of delegating some or all of the steps to team members who have the capacity and desire to help and learn through the process.

t: The Secret Classroom Management Strategy Of Highly Effective Teachers
q: It isn’t applied once and reused when needed. It isn’t a step-by-step, how-to process. I don’t believe it’s ever been revealed in the history of education.
The strategy is this: You decide beforehand how every moment will unfold in your classroom.
Every moment of student behavior/performance/action is decided by YOU.
Because every time your students choose—that is, without your express direction or instruction—your authority drops like an anvil.
The students then are relieved of the stress of decision fatigue.

t: Rejecting Ideas and Proposals Because of the Source
q: The real danger lies in the common bias of rejecting any idea or proposal that comes from a given source.
People expect leaders and decision-makers to operate above their personal feelings and to maintain an impartial and objective lens on all ideas and proposals, no matter where they emanate from.
Yet, this bias, known by the fancy psychological name of reactive devaluation, is tremendously common.
In fact, in many cases, the best leaders may pretend the proposal came from a trusted colleague or third party so they can evaluate it fairly.
Do your best to fight this bias. It has nothing to do with changing your mind about the person, and everything to do with changing your mind about yourself.

t: This Year, No Forklifts
q: Using ChatGPT to complete assignments is like bringing a forklift into the weight room; you will never improve your cognitive fitness that way.

we don’t ask students to write because we need more student writing. The world doesn’t lack for student-written essays; no English teacher has ever assigned an essay on Fahrenheit 451 because they were lacking in such essays. The product of student writing assignments isn’t the point. The byproducts are the point.

What are the byproducts of writing? They are many. Writing produces clarity. It creates mental and volitional strength. It enables inner exploration. It builds knowledge. It makes the mind make meaning. And it does all these things with remarkable efficiency — there is no other learning mode that is like it.
when a student is drowning in assignments and homework, a forklift starts to grow in appeal.
Be mindful of how much you’re assigning students. Overloading them with work will make AI tools tempting, even for students who know the downsides of using AI to complete work.

t: Overcoming Feelings of Intimidation
q: The feeling of being intimidated is uncomfortable at best, and terrifying at worst.
It's important to recognize that intimidation is solely a function of perception and belief.
You can’t be intimidated by anyone or anything unless you give the perceived differences the power to influence the view you have of yourself.
A more unusual approach is to find humor in the situation or person.
The most important idea is to never accept feelings of intimidation.

t: Before Seeking a Win-Win Compromise, Go for a Total-Win Solution
q: Instead of pursuing a win-lose outcome where one party achieves more than the other, decision-making and negotiation experts push the idea of achieving a Win-Win resolution whereby both parties benefit.
Win-Win solutions almost always require concessions on the part of both sides.
But once the solution is put into action, concessions can lead to feelings of resentment, dissatisfaction, and frustration, as sacrifices are seldom perceived to be equally shared.
A Total-Win negotiation stresses the creation of innovative solutions that generate the maximum value for both parties.
When leaders limit themselves to choices that seem reasonable and practical, they often disconnect themselves from what is possible.

t: Lots of Careful and Care-Free Quizzing
q: low-stakes quizzes are a go-to lesson move in whatever courses I teach.
the leader is right — this IS a problem! The kind of effective testing that Benjamin Keep is speaking to isn’t the study guide kind; it’s the “quizzing is just a normal part of what we do” kind.
Students don’t have time or resources to “study” for these quizzes; the quizzes ARE THEIR OWN FORM of studying.

the core misunderstanding that some teachers took away from my session was that they were mapping their own ideas of what a test is — study guides, students given a warning about the test and pressure to study for it — versus the FOR LEARNING nature of tests that Dr. Keep is referencing from the research on retrieval practice.
you do need to be careful about how you present these quizzes and the degree to which they affect a student’s overall grade.

t: Without Realizing It, Leaders Often Displace Their Frustration on Those With Less Power
q: Those on the receiving end of a leader’s extreme frustration typically get defensive, feel disrespected, and seek to protect themselves.
Extreme frustration feeds the urge to behave negatively and aggressively. When the source of the frustration cannot be targeted, any aggression is typically displaced onto unrelated targets.

For instance, a leader extremely frustrated by the pressure to perform from their own manager may believe they cannot express it due to fear of repercussions, so they take out their anger on team or family members.
Displaced frustration is almost always unconscious, which makes it even more problematic.
Good leaders commit to never acting aggressively toward others when they feel frustrated and to acknowledging when their frustrations can't be expressed directly.

t: Peer Groups and the Search for Fresh Ideas
q: For many people, success isn’t what they thought it would be. It fails to bring the lasting happiness and personal fulfillment they expected and counted on.
Highly successful people, to the bewilderment of those around them, often appear lost and rudderless.
They make the pursuit of new ideas the main show, and the success they achieve directly or indirectly becomes the sideshow.

Companies like Vistage, Hampton, Next Monday, Tiger 21, YPO, Matcha, G100, Founders Coach, Entrepreneurs’ Organization, and Admired Leadership facilitate the creation of powerful conversations for committed leaders.
Successful people get together with others like themselves, not only for the connection, camaraderie, and problem sharing, but mostly for the idea generation.

t: The Player-Coach Dilemma
q: You’re managing a team now, and you have responsibility to make people better. As a player-coach, you were excellent as a player and lousy as a coach.

The problem is that they often believe their credibility with the team and across the organization has little to do with their coach role and everything to do with their ability to perform at the highest level.
In practical reality, it is less likely for this to be a 50-50 percentage split, and more effective to pick days where one side of the role gets more time and attention.
Taking the time once a week to explore how each team member is doing and to listen to their concerns and challenges will turn a top player into a solid player-coach.
After all, no one refers to the role as coach-player for a reason.

t: When To Reteach Your Classroom Rules
q: One follows the other like the forming and crashing of a North Shore wave. No hesitating. No reminding. No negotiating.
Once you prove that you’re all-in committed, the testing will stop. Every. Single. Time.
It’s when more than a small few students are misbehaving at the same time.
Either way, they’re misbehaving because they believe you’re a pushover.
Reteach it with double the modeling, double the explicitness, and double the practice. Hammer it home.
